question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch colonial possessions that survived into the 20th century]
options: Dutch East Indies (Indonesia) — The Netherlands' largest colonial territory, comprising Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Celebes, etc.
Suriname — Dutch colony on the northeastern coast of South America
Dutch Antilles — Caribbean island territories including Curaçao and Aruba
Dutch Gold Coast — West African territory retained by the Netherlands as a major colony until 1975
wrong_fact: The Dutch Gold Coast (present-day Ghana) was sold to the British in 1872, not retained until 1975. The Netherlands' primary surviving colonial territories were the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia, independent 1945/1949), Suriname (independent 1975), and the Dutch Antilles/Caribbean islands.
explanation: Dutch East Indies, Suriname, and the Dutch Caribbean (Antilles including Curaçao, Aruba) were genuine long-lasting Dutch possessions. The Dutch Gold Coast was sold to the British in 1872 for a relatively small sum and was not retained as a major Dutch colony into the 20th century. Indonesia gained independence in 1945 (recognised 1949); Suriname in 1975.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Dutch remaining presence in Asia after the loss of Indian territories]
options: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) — Dutch possession ceded to Britain in 1796, formalised by Treaty of Amiens (1802) and 1815
Java — Briefly occupied by the British (1811–1816) during Napoleonic Wars but returned to the Dutch
Malacca — Ceded permanently to the British under Treaty of London (1824)
Formosa (Taiwan) — Dutch possession lost to Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) in 1662, recaptured and held till 1825
wrong_fact: Formosa (Taiwan) was captured from the Dutch by Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) in 1662 and was never recaptured by the Dutch. After the fall of Fort Zeelandia in 1662, the Dutch were permanently expelled from Taiwan and had no further colonial presence there.
explanation: Ceylon was ceded to Britain (occupied 1796, formally 1815). Java was temporarily British (1811–16) under Raffles but returned to Dutch. Malacca was permanently ceded to Britain in 1824. Formosa (Taiwan), however, was lost to Koxinga in 1662 after a 9-month siege, and the Dutch never returned — they did not recapture it or hold it until 1825.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Administrative geography of the Dutch East Indies in the 19th–early 20th century]
options: Batavia (Jakarta) — Capital of the Dutch East Indies, located on the northwestern coast of Java
Borneo — Large island divided between Dutch (south and interior) and British (north) colonial control
Celebes (Sulawesi) — Entire island under Dutch colonial control after the Bone Wars
New Guinea — Eastern half was a joint British-German-Dutch territory divided in the 19th century; Dutch held the western portion
wrong_fact: Celebes (Sulawesi) was NOT entirely under Dutch control after a single 'Bone Wars' — the subjugation of Sulawesi was complex and piecemeal, with the Dutch fighting multiple campaigns including the Bone Wars (1905, 1908). More importantly, the north of Sulawesi around Minahasa was brought under Dutch influence separately and much earlier. 'Entire island under Dutch colonial control' overstates the uniformity of control achieved.
explanation: Batavia on Java's northwest coast was correctly the VOC/Dutch capital. Borneo was genuinely divided between Dutch (Kalimantan) and British (Sarawak, Brunei, British North Borneo) control. New Guinea was partitioned: the Dutch held western New Guinea (West Irian), the Germans held the northeast (Kaiser Wilhelmsland), and the British held the southeast (Papua). Regarding Sulawesi, Dutch control came gradually through multiple campaigns and was never as unified or complete as 'entire island' implies — particularly, the Bone Wars of 1905–08 were the final subjugation of the Bugis south, but earlier treaties and arrangements varied by region.
